steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Below is a “big-picture” tour of the Transformer model, stripped of most math but rich in the key ideas. Read it as a narrative of how information flows through the network and why each architectural choice exists.

----------------------------------------------------------------
1. The problem that motivates Transformers
----------------------------------------------------------------
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and their gated variants (LSTM, GRU) process sequences token-by-token. They are hard to parallelise and struggle with long-range dependencies because distant information must be squeezed through a single hidden state. Transformers solve both issues by replacing recurrence with an attention mechanism that can look at the whole sequence at once, in parallel.

----------------------------------------------------------------
2. The data format: from tokens to vectors
----------------------------------------------------------------
• Tokenisation. Text (or any discrete sequence) is split into tokens such as words, sub-words, characters, etc.

• Embedding. Each token id is converted to a dense vector e.g. 768-D. At this point every token is represented independently, so order information is still missing.

• Positional encoding. Because we discarded explicit order, we add a position signal to each embedding. This signal can be:
  – Fixed sinusoidal functions (original paper).
  – Learned position embeddings (often used in practice).
  Now the model can distinguish “cat sat” from “sat cat”.

----------------------------------------------------------------
3. Self-attention: the central invention
----------------------------------------------------------------
Goal: For every position i, compute a context-aware vector that is a weighted blend of the other positions’ vectors. In effect, each token asks: “Which other tokens in the sentence are relevant to me?”

Mechanism:
1. For each token vector xᵢ create three derived vectors by learned linear projections:
   • Query qᵢ
   • Key   kᵢ
   • Value vᵢ
2. Similarity scores: Align a token’s query with every key in the sequence using a (scaled) dot product: score(i,j) = qᵢ · kⱼ / √dₖ.
3. Softmax: Convert the list of scores for token i into weights that sum to 1.
4. Weighted sum: Multiply every value vⱼ by its weight and add them. Result = new vector zᵢ for position i.

Interpretation: qᵢ is “what I’m looking for”, kⱼ describes “what I contain”, vⱼ is the content to retrieve if you deem me relevant. Self-attention is differentiable, learnable, and re-computes these relationships in every layer, allowing the model to dynamically build dependency graphs (syntax, coreference, topic) without any hand-crafted rules.

----------------------------------------------------------------
4. Multi-head attention: looking through several lenses
----------------------------------------------------------------
Instead of doing one attention calculation on large vectors, split the space into h smaller sub-spaces (heads). Each head can specialise:
  – One head might focus on subject-verb agreement.
  – Another might capture coreference.
Concatenate the h heads and linearly project back to the original dimension. This adds only modest cost yet greatly increases modelling capacity.

----------------------------------------------------------------
5. Layer structure: what a single Transformer block looks like
----------------------------------------------------------------
For an encoder (BERT-style):
  a) Multi-head self-attention
     + Add & Norm (residual connection + layer norm)
  b) Position-wise feed-forward network (two linear layers with a non-linearity, applied identically to every position)
     + Add & Norm

Residuals allow gradients to flow; LayerNorm stabilises training.

For a decoder (GPT-style):
  – Same as above but with an added causal mask so each position only attends to previous positions (enforcing autoregressive generation).

For the original sequence-to-sequence Transformer (e.g. machine translation):
  • Encoder block(s): self-attention + FFN
  • Decoder block(s): 
        1. Masked self-attention (look only left)
        2. Cross-attention (queries come from decoder, keys/values come from encoder outputs → lets the decoder attend to the source sentence)
        3. FFN
  Each sub-layer again wrapped with residual + layernorm.

----------------------------------------------------------------
6. Stacking layers: deep context
----------------------------------------------------------------
Stack N identical blocks (6–96+ in modern models). Early layers learn local/syntactic relations, deeper layers encode high-level semantics. The final set of vectors (one per token) now embed rich context from the entire sequence.

----------------------------------------------------------------
7. Output heads
----------------------------------------------------------------
• For language modelling (GPT): Pass the final decoder vectors through a linear layer tied to the embedding matrix, softmax to produce a probability distribution over the next token.

• For classification (BERT): Use a special [CLS] token’s final vector, feed it to a classifier.

• For translation (original Transformer): Decoder emits one token at a time, feeding predictions back in until an <eos> token appears.

----------------------------------------------------------------
8. Why it works
----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Parallelism: Self-attention sees the whole sequence simultaneously, enabling efficient GPU/TPU usage.
2. Direct long-range paths: Any token can influence any other in a single hop; path length is O(1) vs O(n) for RNNs.
3. Adaptive computation: Heads decide on-the-fly what to focus on; no fixed window or kernel like CNNs.
4. Scalability: Model size can be increased (width, depth, heads) and trained on massive corpora, yielding dramatic performance jumps (Scaling Laws).

----------------------------------------------------------------
9. Key training tricks (conceptual)
----------------------------------------------------------------
• Masking. For BERT-like pre-training, randomly mask tokens and train to predict them (bidirectional context learning).
• Causal language modelling. For GPT, predict the next token, using only previous context.
• Dropout and attention dropout for regularisation.
• Label smoothing for translation tasks.
• Learning rate warm-up with Adam/AdamW optimisers.

----------------------------------------------------------------
10. Limitations & evolutions
----------------------------------------------------------------
• Quadratic cost: Attention over n tokens costs O(n²) memory/time. Long-context variants (Longformer, Reformer, Performer) introduce sparse or low-rank approximations.
• No inherent recurrence or state: Must re-process the full context each step, though caching helps in inference.
• Data hunger: Effectiveness grows with scale—requires large corpora and compute.
• Positional generalisation: Sinusoidal embeddings extrapolate poorly to unseen lengths; relative position encodings (T5, Transformer-XL, ALiBi) mitigate this.

----------------------------------------------------------------
11. The essence, in one paragraph
----------------------------------------------------------------
A Transformer treats a sequence as a set of vectors that repeatedly ask one another how relevant they are. Through multi-head self-attention each token builds a bespoke, weighted summary of the entire sequence, layer after layer, while residual paths and feed-forward sub-nets refine the representation. This attention-driven, fully parallel approach sidesteps the bottlenecks of recurrence, scales elegantly, and has become the foundation for modern NLP, vision, audio, and multi-modal models.
